title: Precipitation and Dissolution
lead: A sparingly soluble ionic solid in contact with its saturated solution is an equilibrium of its own. This section writes the equilibrium constant for that dissolution, the solubility product, relates it to how much of the solid dissolves, and uses it to predict when a precipitate forms, to separate ions, and to account for the effect of an ion the solution already contains.
objectives: Write chemical equations and equilibrium expressions representing solubility equilibria
Carry out equilibrium computations involving solubility, equilibrium expressions, and solute concentrations
summary_html:
The equilibrium constant for an equilibrium involving the precipitation or dissolution of a slightly soluble ionic solid is called the solubility product, $\kKsp$, of the solid. For a heterogeneous equilibrium involving the slightly soluble solid MpXq and its ions Mm+ and Xn–:

$$\text{M}_{p}\text{X}_{q}(s)\rightleftharpoons p\text{M}^{m+}(aq)+q\text{X}^{n-}(aq)$$

the solubility product expression is:

$$\kKsp={\kconcMion}^{p}{\kconcXion}^{q}$$

The solubility product of a slightly soluble electrolyte can be calculated from its solubility; conversely, its solubility can be calculated from its $\kKsp$, provided the only significant reaction that occurs when the solid dissolves is the formation of its ions.

A slightly soluble electrolyte begins to precipitate when the magnitude of the reaction quotient for the dissolution reaction exceeds the magnitude of the solubility product. Precipitation continues until the reaction quotient equals the solubility product.

figures.original_caption: Silver chloride is a sparingly soluble ionic solid. When it is added to water, it dissolves slightly and produces a mixture consisting of a very dilute solution of Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in equilibrium with undissolved silver chloride.

exercises.prompt:
Write the dissolution equation and the solubility product for each of the following slightly soluble compounds:
(a) BaSO4
(b) Ag2SO4
(c) Al(OH)3
(d) Pb(OH)Cl

In a saturated solution of Mg(OH)2, the concentration of Mg2+ is 1.31 × 10–4 M. What is the solubility product for Mg(OH)2?
${\text{Mg(OH)}}_{2}(s)\rightleftharpoons {\text{Mg}}^{\text{2+}}(aq)+{\text{2OH}}^{\text{−}}(aq)$

answer.hint: The dissolution gives two OH− for each Mg2+, so [OH−] is twice [Mg2+]; then Ksp = [Mg2+][OH−]2.

exercises.prompt: The Ksp of AgI is 1.5 × 10–16. Calculate the molar solubility of silver iodide.

answer.hint: AgI gives one Ag+ and one I−, so Ksp = x2.

exercises.prompt: The Ksp of PbI2 is 1.4 × 10–8. Calculate the molar solubility of lead(II) iodide.

answer.hint: PbI2 gives x of Pb2+ and 2x of I−, so Ksp = 4x3.

exercises.prompt: The solubility of TlCl [thallium(I) chloride], an intermediate formed when thallium is being isolated from ores, is 3.12 grams per liter at 20 °C. What is its solubility product?

answer.hint: Convert 3.12 g/L to a molar solubility with the molar mass of TlCl; both ion concentrations equal it.

exercises.prompt: Determine the molar solubility of MgF2 from its solubility product: Ksp = 6.4 × 10–9.

answer.hint: Ksp = [Mg2+][F−]2 = (x)(2x)2 = 4x3.

exercises.prompt: Predict whether CaHPO4 will precipitate from a solution with [Ca2+] = 0.0001 M and $[{\text{HPO}}_{4}{}^{\text{2−}}]$ = 0.001 M.

answer.hint: Compare Q = [Ca2+][HPO42−] with the Ksp of CaHPO4 in Appendix J.
answer.solution: No precipitation of CaHPO4; Q = 1 × 10–7, which is less than Ksp (7 × 10–7)

exercises.prompt: Will KClO4 precipitate when 20 mL of a 0.050-M solution of K+ is added to 80 mL of a 0.50-M solution of ${\text{ClO}}_{4}{}^{\text{−}}?$ (Hint: Use the dilution equation to calculate the concentrations of potassium and perchlorate ions in the mixture.)

answer.hint: Both solutions are diluted to 100 mL; find [K+] and [ClO4−] in the mixture, then compare Q with Ksp.

exercises.prompt: If a solution contains 0.0020 mol of ${\text{CrO}}_{4}{}^{\text{2−}}$ per liter, what concentration of Ag<sup>+</sup> ion must be reached by adding solid AgNO<sub>3</sub> before Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> begins to precipitate? Neglect any increase in volume upon adding the solid silver nitrate.

answer.hint: Set Ksp = [Ag+]2[CrO42−] and solve for [Ag+].

exercises.prompt: The first step in the preparation of magnesium metal is the precipitation of Mg(OH)2 from sea water by the addition of Ca(OH)2. The concentration of Mg2+(aq) in sea water is 5.37 × 10–2 M. Calculate the pH at which [Mg2+] is decreased to 1.0 × 10–5 M

answer.hint: Find [OH−] from Ksp = [Mg2+][OH−]2 with [Mg2+] = 1.0 × 10−5 M, then pOH and pH.

exercises.prompt: If silver nitrate solution is added to a solution which is 0.050 M in both Cl– and Br– ions, at what [Ag+] would precipitation begin, and what would be the formula of the precipitate?

answer.hint: With equal halide concentrations, the salt with the smaller Ksp needs the lower [Ag+]; divide its Ksp by 0.050 M.

exercises.prompt:
What is the effect on the amount of solid NiCO3 and the concentrations of Ni2+ and ${\text{CO}}_{3}{}^{\text{2−}}$ when each of the following are added to a saturated solution of NiCO3
(a) Ni(NO3)2
(b) KClO4
(c) NiCO3
(d) K2CO3

answer.solution: (a) mass of NiCO3(s) increases, [Ni2+] increases, $[{\text{CO}}_{3}{}^{\text{2−}}]$ decreases; (b) no appreciable effect; (c) no effect except to increase the amount of solid NiCO3; (d) mass of NiCO3(s) increases, [Ni2+] decreases, $[{\text{CO}}_{3}{}^{\text{2−}}]$ increases;

exercises.prompt: Calculate the molar solubility of aluminum hydroxide, Al(OH)3, in a 0.015-M solution of aluminum nitrate, Al(NO3)3. The Ksp of Al(OH)3 is 2 × 10–32.

answer.hint: Take [Al3+] ≈ 0.015 M and [OH−] = 3x, so Ksp = (0.015)(3x)3.

exercises.prompt:
Complete the changes in concentrations for each of the following reactions:
(a)
$\begin{array}{lll}\text{AgI}(s)\;\longrightarrow \; & {\text{Ag}}^{\text{+}}\;(aq) & +\;{\text{I}}^{\text{−}}(aq) \\ \\ & x & \_\_\_\_\_\end{array}$
(b)
$\begin{array}{lll}{\text{CaCO}}_{3}(s)\;\longrightarrow \; & {\text{Ca}}^{\text{2+}}(aq)+ & {\text{CO}}_{3}{}^{\text{2−}}(aq) \\ \\ & \_\_\_\_ & x\end{array}$
(c)
$\begin{array}{lll}\text{Mg}{(\text{OH})}_{2}(s)\;\longrightarrow \; & {\text{Mg}}^{\text{2+}}(aq)+ & 2{\text{OH}}^{\text{−}}(aq) \\ \\ & x & \_\_\_\_\_\end{array}$
(d)
$\begin{array}{lll}{\text{Mg}}_{3}({\text{PO}}_{4}{)}_{2}(s)\;\longrightarrow \; & 3{\text{Mg}}^{\text{2+}}(aq)+ & 2{\text{PO}}_{4}{}^{\text{3−}}(aq) \\ \\ & x & \_\_\_\_\_\end{array}$
(e)
$\begin{array}{llll}{\text{Ca}}_{5}({\text{PO}}_{4}{)}_{3}\text{OH}(s)\;\longrightarrow \; & 5{\text{Ca}}^{\text{2+}}(aq)+ & 3{\text{PO}}_{4}{}^{\text{3−}}(aq)+ & {\text{OH}}^{\text{−}}(aq) \\ \\ & \_\_\_\_\_ & \_\_\_\_\_ & x\end{array}$

Complete the changes in concentrations for each of the following reactions:
(a)
$\begin{array}{lll}{\text{BaSO}}_{4}(s)\;\longrightarrow \; & {\text{Ba}}^{\text{2+}}(aq)+ & {\text{SO}}_{4}{}^{\text{2−}}(aq) \\ \\ & x & \_\_\_\_\_\end{array}$
(b
$\begin{array}{lll}{\text{Ag}}_{2}{\text{SO}}_{4}(s)\;\longrightarrow \; & 2{\text{Ag}}^{\text{+}}(aq)+ & {\text{SO}}_{4}{}^{\text{2−}}(aq) \\ \\ & \_\_\_\_\_ & x\end{array}$
(c)
$\begin{array}{lll}\text{Al}{(\text{OH})}_{3}(s)\;\longrightarrow \; & {\text{Al}}^{\text{3+}}(aq)+ & 3{\text{OH}}^{\text{−}}(aq) \\ \\ & x & \_\_\_\_\_\end{array}$
(d)
$\begin{array}{llll}\text{Pb}(\text{OH})\text{Cl}(s)\;\longrightarrow \; & {\text{Pb}}^{\text{2+}}(aq)+ & {\text{OH}}^{\text{−}}(aq)+ & {\text{Cl}}^{\text{−}}(aq) \\ \\ & \_\_\_\_\_\; & x & \_\_\_\_\_\end{array}$
(e)
$\begin{array}{lll}{\text{Ca}}_{3}({\text{AsO}}_{4}{)}_{2}(s)\;\longrightarrow \; & 3{\text{Ca}}^{\text{2+}}(aq)+ & 2{\text{AsO}}_{4}{}^{\text{3−}}(aq) \\ \\ & 3x & \_\_\_\_\_\end{array}$

answer.solution: Suggested approach: each ion’s change is its coefficient in the dissolution equation times the molar solubility. From the change you are given, find the molar solubility by dividing by that ion’s coefficient, then multiply by the other ion’s coefficient.

exercises.prompt: How do the concentrations of Ag<sup>+</sup> and ${\text{CrO}}_{4}{}^{\text{2−}}$ in a saturated solution above 1.0 g of solid Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> change when 100 g of solid Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> is added to the system? Explain.

answer.solution: There is no change. A solid has an activity of 1 whether there is a little or a lot.

exercises.prompt: How do the concentrations of Pb<sup>2+</sup> and S<sup>2–</sup> change when K<sub>2</sub>S is added to a saturated solution of PbS?

answer.solution: Suggested approach: write the dissolution equation of PbS and name the ion that K<sub>2</sub>S adds. Decide which way that addition shifts the equilibrium, and what the shift does to the concentration of each ion.

exercises.prompt: What additional information do we need to answer the following question: How is the equilibrium of solid silver bromide with a saturated solution of its ions affected when the temperature is raised?

answer.solution: The solubility of silver bromide at the new temperature must be known. Normally the solubility increases and some of the solid silver bromide will dissolve.

exercises.prompt: Which of the following slightly soluble compounds has a solubility greater than that calculated from its solubility product because of hydrolysis of the anion present: CoSO<sub>3</sub>, CuI, PbCO<sub>3</sub>, PbCl<sub>2</sub>, Tl<sub>2</sub>S, KClO<sub>4</sub>?

answer.solution: Suggested approach: an anion that is the conjugate base of a weak acid reacts with water, which lowers its concentration and lets more of the solid dissolve. For each compound, decide whether its anion is the conjugate base of a weak acid or of a strong one.

exercises.prompt: Which of the following slightly soluble compounds has a solubility greater than that calculated from its solubility product because of hydrolysis of the anion present: AgCl, BaSO<sub>4</sub>, CaF<sub>2</sub>, Hg<sub>2</sub>I<sub>2</sub>, MnCO<sub>3</sub>, and ZnS?

Write the ionic equation for dissolution and the solubility product (Ksp) expression for each of the following slightly soluble ionic compounds:
(a) PbCl2
(b) Ag2S
(c) Sr3(PO4)2
(d) SrSO4

answer.solution: Suggested approach: write each compound’s ions with their charges and the coefficients that balance the formula. Each coefficient becomes the exponent of that ion’s concentration in the Ksp expression, and the solid does not appear in it.

exercises.prompt:
Write the ionic equation for the dissolution and the Ksp expression for each of the following slightly soluble ionic compounds:
(a) LaF3
(b) CaCO3
(c) Ag2SO4
(d) Pb(OH)2

The Handbook of Chemistry and Physics gives solubilities of the following compounds in grams per 100 mL of water. Because these compounds are only slightly soluble, assume that the volume does not change on dissolution and calculate the solubility product for each.
(a) BaSeO4, 0.0118 g/100 mL
(b) Ba(BrO3)2·H2O, 0.30 g/100 mL
(c) NH4MgAsO4·6H2O, 0.038 g/100 mL
(d) La2(MoO4)3, 0.00179 g/100 mL

parts.hint: Convert grams per 100 mL to moles per liter with each molar mass, then write the ion concentrations from the formula.

exercises.prompt: Use solubility products and predict which of the following salts is the most soluble, in terms of moles per liter, in pure water: CaF<sub>2</sub>, Hg<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>, PbI<sub>2</sub>, or Sn(OH)<sub>2</sub>.

answer.solution: Suggested approach: look up each Ksp in Appendix J and write it in terms of the molar solubility x. Where every salt gives the same numbers of cations and anions, the order of the Ksp values is the order of the molar solubilities; where they do not, solve for each x and compare those.

exercises.prompt:
Assuming that no equilibria other than dissolution are involved, calculate the molar solubility of each of the following from its solubility product:
(a) KHC4H4O6
(b) PbI2
(c) Ag4[Fe(CN)6], a salt containing the ${\text{Fe(CN)}}_{6}{}^{\text{4–}}$ ion
(d) Hg2I2

parts.hint: Take each Ksp from Appendix J and write it in terms of x from the dissolution equation.

exercises.prompt:
Assuming that no equilibria other than dissolution are involved, calculate the concentration of all solute species in each of the following solutions of salts in contact with a solution containing a common ion. Show that changes in the initial concentrations of the common ions can be neglected.
(a) AgCl(s) in 0.025 M NaCl
(b) CaF2(s) in 0.00133 M KF
(c) Ag2SO4(s) in 0.500 L of a solution containing 19.50 g of K2SO4
(d) Zn(OH)2(s) in a solution buffered at a pH of 11.45

parts.hint: Take the common ion’s concentration as its initial value and solve Ksp for the other ion.

answer.solution:
(a) 6.4 × 10−9 M = [Ag+], [Cl−] = 0.025 M. Check: $\frac{6.4\;\times \;{10}^{-9}\;M}{0.025\;M}\;\times \;\text{100\%}=\text{2.6}\;\times \;{10}^{-5}\%,$an insignificant change;
(b) 2.2 × 10−5 M = [Ca2+], [F−] = 0.0013 M. Check: $\frac{\text{2.26}\;\times \;{10}^{-5}\;M}{0.00133\;M}\;\times \;\text{100\%}=\text{1.70\%}.$ This value is less than 5% and can be ignored.
(c) 0.2238 M = $[{\text{SO}}_{4}{}^{2\text{−}}];$ [Ag+] = 7.4 × 10–3 M. Check: $\frac{3.7\;\times \;{10}^{-3}}{0.2238}\;\times \;100\%=\text{1.64}\;\times \;{10}^{-2};$ the condition is satisfied.
(d) [OH–] = 2.8 × 10–3 M; 5.7 × 10−12 M = [Zn2+]. Check: $\frac{5.7\;\times \;{10}^{-12}}{2.8\;\times \;{10}^{-3}}\;\times \;\text{100\%}=\text{2.0}\;\times \;{10}^{-7}\%;$ x is less than 5% of [OH–] and is, therefore, negligible.

exercises.prompt:
Assuming that no equilibria other than dissolution are involved, calculate the concentration of all solute species in each of the following solutions of salts in contact with a solution containing a common ion. State whether or not it is appropriate to neglect the changes in the initial concentrations of the common ions.
(a) TlCl(s) in 0.025 M TlNO3
(b) BaF2(s) in 0.313 M KF
(c) MgC2O4 in 2.250 L of a solution containing 8.156 g of Mg(NO3)2
(d) Ca(OH)2(s) in an unbuffered solution initially with a pH of 12.700

parts.hint: In (a) the change is not small next to 0.025 M, so solve the quadratic; in the others take the common ion at its initial value.

answer.solution:
(a) The change in initial concentration of common ion may not be neglected (must solve quadratic equation)
[Ti+] =0.031 M
[Cl–] = 0.0056 M (b) The change in initial concentration of common ion may be neglected.
[Ba2+] = 2.4 × 10–4 M
[F–] = 0.313 M;
(c) The change in initial concentration of common ion may be neglected.
[Mg2+] = 0.0244 M
$[{\text{C}}_{2}{\text{O}}_{4}{}^{\text{2−}}]=2.9\;\times \;{10}^{\text{−5}}\;M$
(d) The change in initial concentration of common ion may be neglected.
[Ca2+] = 5.18 × 10–4 M
[C2)42–] = 0.051 M

exercises.prompt: Explain why the changes in concentrations of the common ions in Exercise 15.17 can be neglected.

answer.solution: Suggested approach: in each part of Exercise 15.17, compare the change x with the initial concentration of the common ion. A change of less than about 5% of that concentration leaves it essentially unchanged and can be neglected.

exercises.prompt: Explain why the changes in concentrations of the common ions in Exercise 15.18 cannot be neglected.

answer.solution: The changes in concentration are greater than 5% and thus exceed the maximum value for disregarding the change.

exercises.prompt: Refer to Appendix J for solubility products for calcium salts. Determine which of the calcium salts listed is most soluble in moles per liter and which is most soluble in grams per liter.

answer.solution: CaSO<sub>4</sub>∙2H<sub>2</sub>O is the most soluble Ca salt in mol/L, and it is also the most soluble Ca salt in g/L.

exercises.prompt: Public Health Service standards for drinking water set a maximum of 250 mg/L (2.60 × 10–3 M) of ${\text{SO}}_{4}{}^{\text{2−}}$ because of its cathartic action (it is a laxative). Does natural water that is saturated with CaSO4 (“gyp” water) as a result or passing through soil containing gypsum, CaSO4·2H2O, meet these standards? What is the concentration of ${\text{SO}}_{4}{}^{\text{2−}}$ in such water?

answer.hint: In gyp water [Ca2+] = [SO42−] = x, and Ksp of CaSO4·2H2O = x2; compare x with 2.60 × 10−3 M.
answer.solution: 7.8 × 10–3 M = $[{\text{SO}}_{4}{}^{\text{2−}}]$ = [Ca2+]; Since this concentration is higher than 2.60 × 10–3 M, “gyp” water does not meet the standards.

exercises.prompt: The solubility product of CaSO4·2H2O is 2.4 × 10–5. What mass of this salt will dissolve in 1.0 L of 0.010 M ${\text{SO}}_{4}{}^{\text{2−}}?$

answer.hint: [Ca2+] = x and [SO42−] = 0.010 + x; solve, then convert x moles to grams of the dihydrate.

exercises.prompt:
Assuming that no equilibria other than dissolution are involved, calculate the concentrations of ions in a saturated solution of each of the following (see Appendix J for solubility products):
(a) AgI
(b) Ag2SO4
(c) Mn(OH)2
(d) Sr(OH)2·8H2O
(e) the mineral brucite, Mg(OH)2

parts.hint: Write each Ksp from Appendix J in terms of x, solve, and multiply by each ion’s coefficient.

exercises.prompt:
The following concentrations are found in mixtures of ions in equilibrium with slightly soluble solids. From the concentrations given, calculate Ksp for each of the slightly soluble solids indicated:
(a) TlCl: [Tl+] = 1.21 × 10–2 M, [Cl–] = 1.2 × 10–2 M
(b) Ce(IO3)4: [Ce4+] = 1.8 × 10–4 M, $[{\text{IO}}_{3}{}^{\text{−}}]$ = 2.6 × 10–13 M
(c) Gd2(SO4)3: [Gd3+] = 0.132 M, $[{\text{SO}}_{\text{4}}{}^{\text{2−}}]$ = 0.198 M
(d) Ag2SO4: [Ag+] = 2.40 × 10–2 M, $[{\text{SO}}_{\text{4}}{}^{\text{2−}}]$ = 2.05 × 10–2 M
(e) BaSO4: [Ba2+] = 0.500 M, $[{\text{SO}}_{\text{4}}{}^{\text{2−}}]$ = 2.16 × 10−10 M

parts.hint: Raise each concentration to the power of its coefficient in the formula and multiply.

exercises.prompt:
Which of the following compounds precipitates from a solution that has the concentrations indicated? (See Appendix J for Ksp values.)
(a) CaCO3: [Ca2+] = 0.003 M, $[{\text{CO}}_{\text{3}}{}^{\text{2−}}]$ = 0.003 M
(b) Co(OH)2: [Co2+] = 0.01 M, [OH–] = 1 × 10–7 M
(c) CaHPO4: [Ca2+] = 0.01 M, $[{\text{HPO}}_{\text{4}}{}^{\text{2−}}]$ = 2 × 10–6 M
(d) Pb3(PO4)2: [Pb2+] = 0.01 M, $[{\text{PO}}_{\text{4}}{}^{\text{3−}}]$= 1 × 10–13 M

answer.solution: (a) CaCO<sub>3</sub> does precipitate. (b) The compound does not precipitate. (c) The compound does not precipitate. (d) The compound precipitates.

exercises.prompt: Calculate the concentration of sulfate ion when BaSO4 just begins to precipitate from a solution that is 0.0758 M in Ba2+.

answer.hint: Set Q = Ksp = [Ba2+][SO42−] with [Ba2+] = 0.0758 M.

exercises.prompt: Calculate the concentration of ${\text{PO}}_{4}{}^{\text{3−}}$ when Ag3PO4 starts to precipitate from a solution that is 0.0125 M in Ag+.

answer.hint: Ksp = [Ag+]3[PO43−]; solve for the phosphate concentration.

exercises.prompt: Calculate the concentration of Ag+ required to begin precipitation of Ag2CO3 in a solution that is 2.50 × 10–6 M in ${\text{CO}}_{3}{}^{\text{2−}}.$

answer.hint: Ksp = [Ag+]2[CO32−]; solve for [Ag+].

exercises.prompt: What [F–] is required to reduce [Ca2+] to 1.0 × 10–4 M by precipitation of CaF2?

answer.hint: Ksp = [Ca2+][F−]2 with [Ca2+] = 1.0 × 10−4 M.

exercises.prompt:
Perform these calculations for nickel(II) carbonate. (a) With what volume of water must a precipitate containing NiCO3 be washed to dissolve 0.100 g of this compound? Assume that the wash water becomes saturated with NiCO3 (Ksp = 1.36 × 10–7).
(b) If the NiCO3 were a contaminant in a sample of CoCO3 (Ksp = 1.0 × 10–12), what mass of CoCO3 would have been lost? Keep in mind that both NiCO3 and CoCO3 dissolve in the same solution.

parts.hint: Find the molar solubility of NiCO<sub>3</sub>, then the volume that holds 0.100 g of it.

exercises.prompt: A solution is 0.010 M in both Cu2+ and Cd2+. What percentage of Cd2+ remains in the solution when 99.9% of the Cu2+ has been precipitated as CuS by adding sulfide?

answer.hint: Find [S2−] when 0.1% of the Cu2+ remains, then compare [Cd2+][S2−] with the Ksp of CdS.

exercises.prompt:
What reagent might be used to separate the ions in each of the following mixtures, which are 0.1 M with respect to each ion? In some cases it may be necessary to control the pH. (Hint: Consider the Ksp values given in Appendix J.)
(a) ${\text{Hg}}_{2}{}^{\text{2+}}$ and Cu2+
(b) ${\text{SO}}_{4}{}^{\text{2−}}$ and Cl–
(c) Hg2+ and Co2+
(d) Zn2+ and Sr2+
(e) Ba2+ and Mg2+
(f) ${\text{CO}}_{3}{}^{\text{2−}}$ and OH–

answer.solution: (a) ${\text{Hg}}_{2}{}^{\text{2+}}$ and Cu2+: Add ${\text{SO}}_{4}{}^{\text{2−}}.$ (b) ${\text{SO}}_{4}{}^{\text{2−}}$ and Cl–: Add Ba2+. (c) Hg2+ and Co2+: Add S2–. (d) Zn2+ and Sr2+: Add OH– until [OH–] = 0.050 M. (e) Ba2+ and Mg2+: Add ${\text{SO}}_{4}{}^{\text{2−}}.$ (f) ${\text{CO}}_{3}{}^{\text{2−}}$ and OH–: Add Ba2+.

exercises.prompt: A solution contains 1.0 × 10<sup>–5</sup> mol of KBr and 0.10 mol of KCl per liter. AgNO<sub>3</sub> is gradually added to this solution. Which forms first, solid AgBr or solid AgCl?

answer.solution: Suggested approach: as in Example 15.11, find the [Ag+] at which each salt begins to precipitate, its Ksp from Appendix J divided by the concentration of its halide ion. The salt that needs the lower [Ag+] forms first.

exercises.prompt: A solution contains 1.0 × 10<sup>–2</sup> mol of KI and 0.10 mol of KCl per liter. AgNO<sub>3</sub> is gradually added to this solution. Which forms first, solid AgI or solid AgCl?

answer.hint: Compare the [Ag+] at which each salt begins to precipitate: its Ksp divided by its halide concentration.

exercises.prompt: About 50% of urinary calculi (kidney stones) consist of calcium phosphate, Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>. The normal mid range calcium content excreted in the urine is 0.10 g of Ca<sup>2+</sup> per day. The normal mid range amount of urine passed may be taken as 1.4 L per day. What is the maximum concentration of phosphate ion that urine can contain before a calculus begins to form?

answer.hint: Convert 0.10 g of Ca2+ in 1.4 L to a molarity, then solve Ksp = [Ca2+]3[PO43−]2.

exercises.prompt:
Magnesium metal (a component of alloys used in aircraft and a reducing agent used in the production of uranium, titanium, and other active metals) is isolated from sea water by the following sequence of reactions:
${\text{Mg}}^{\text{2+}}(aq)+{\text{Ca(OH)}}_{2}(aq)\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{Mg(OH)}}_{2}(s)+{\text{Ca}}^{\text{2+}}(aq)$
${\text{Mg(OH)}}_{2}(s)+\text{2HCl(}aq)\;\longrightarrow \;{\text{MgCl}}_{2}(s)+{\text{2H}}_{2}\text{O}(l)$

Sea water has a density of 1.026 g/cm3 and contains 1272 parts per million of magnesium as Mg2+(aq) by mass. What mass, in kilograms, of Ca(OH)2 is required to precipitate 99.9% of the magnesium in 1.00 × 103 L of sea water?

exercises.prompt:
The carbonate ion concentration is gradually increased in a solution containing equal concentrations of the divalent cations of magnesium, calcium, strontium, barium, and manganese. Which of the following carbonates will precipitate first? Which will precipitate last? Explain.
(a) ${\text{MgCO}}_{3}\bullet 3{\text{H}}_{2}\text{O}\hspace{4em}{K}_{\text{sp}}=1\;\times \;1{0}^{-5}$
(b) ${\text{CaCO}}_{3}\hspace{4em}{K}_{\text{sp}}=8.7\;\times \;1{0}^{-9}$
(c) ${\text{SrCO}}_{3}\hspace{4em}{K}_{\text{sp}}=7\;\times \;1{0}^{-10}$
(d) ${\text{BaCO}}_{3}\hspace{4em}{K}_{\text{sp}}=1.6\;\times \;1{0}^{-9}$
(e) ${\text{MnCO}}_{3}\hspace{4em}{K}_{\text{sp}}=8.8\;\times \;1{0}^{-11}$

answer.solution: MnCO3 will form first since it has the smallest Ksp value among these homologous compounds and is therefore the least soluble. MgCO3•3H2O will be the last to precipitate since it has the largest K_sp value and is the most soluble. Ksp value.

exercises.prompt: Under what circumstances, if any, does a sample of solid AgCl completely dissolve in pure water?

answer.solution: when the amount of solid is so small that a saturated solution is not produced

exercises.prompt: A saturated solution of a slightly soluble electrolyte in contact with some of the solid electrolyte is said to be a system in equilibrium. Explain. Why is such a system called a heterogeneous equilibrium?

answer.solution: Suggested approach: describe what happens at the surface of the solid in a saturated solution, and compare the rates at which ions leave it and return to it. Then count the phases present and recall what an equilibrium with components in more than one phase is called.

exercises.prompt:
The following question is taken from a Chemistry Advanced Placement Examination and is used with the permission of the Educational Testing Service.
Solve the following problem:
${\text{MgF}}_{2}(s)\rightleftharpoons {\text{Mg}}^{\text{2+}}(aq)+2{\text{F}}^{\text{−}}(aq)$
In a saturated solution of MgF2 at 18 °C, the concentration of Mg2+ is 1.21 × 10–3 M. The equilibrium is represented by the preceding equation.
(a) Write the expression for the solubility-product constant, Ksp, and calculate its value at 18 °C.
(b) Calculate the equilibrium concentration of Mg2+ in 1.000 L of saturated MgF2 solution at 18 °C to which 0.100 mol of solid KF has been added. The KF dissolves completely. Assume the volume change is negligible.
(c) Predict whether a precipitate of MgF2 will form when 100.0 mL of a 3.00 × 10–3-M solution of Mg(NO3)2 is mixed with 200.0 mL of a 2.00 × 10–3-M solution of NaF at 18 °C. Show the calculations to support your prediction.
(d) At 27 °C the concentration of Mg2+ in a saturated solution of MgF2 is 1.17 × 10–3 M. Is the dissolving of MgF2 in water an endothermic or an exothermic process? Give an explanation to support your conclusion.

answer.solution:
(a) Ksp = [Mg2+][F–]2 = (1.21 × 10–3)(2 × 1.21 × 10–3)2 = 7.09 × 10–9
(b) 7.09 × 10–7 M
(c) Determine the concentration of Mg2+ and F– that will be present in the final volume. Compare the value of the ion product [Mg2+][F–]2 with Ksp. If this value is larger than Ksp, precipitation will occur.
0.1000 L × 3.00 × 10–3 M Mg(NO3)2 = 0.3000 L × M Mg(NO3)2
M Mg(NO3)2 = 1.00 × 10–3 M
0.2000 L × 2.00 × 10–3 M NaF = 0.3000 L × M NaF
M NaF = 1.33 × 10–3 M
ion product = (1.00 × 10–3)(1.33 × 10–3)2 = 1.77 × 10–9 This value is smaller than Ksp, so no precipitation will occur.
(d) MgF2 is less soluble at 27 °C than at 18 °C. Because added heat acts like an added reagent, when it appears on the product side, the Le Châtelier’s principle states that the equilibrium will shift to the reactants’ side to counter the stress. Consequently, less reagent will dissolve. This situation is found in our case. Therefore, the reaction is exothermic.
